The Dunnock (Prunella modularis) begins life as a remarkably small hatchling, with newly emerged altricial chicks typically weighing just 1.7 grams [Wwb = 1.7 grams] at birth, a modest initial mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves required to sustain the embryo through the later stages of organogenesis. At an incubation temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the embryonated egg develops for an average of 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days] before the chick begins to pip the calcareous shell. This developmental duration, measured under stable captive conditions, is consistent with the incubation periods reported for other small altricial passerines of the family Prunellidae. Field studies have confirmed that the timing of hatching is tightly linked to ambient temperature, with cooler spring temperatures occasionally extending the incubation phase by a day or two beyond the average recorded at a stable 34 °C. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, approximately 2.13 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.13 grams], provides the entire nutritional basis for the developing amniote embryo until exogenous feeding begins.

During the nestling stage, the altricial Dunnock chick undergoes a rapid phase of mass gain, with the 1.7 gram [Wwb = 1.7 gram] natal mass serving as the baseline from which nestlings must more than decuple their body weight before fledging, a hallmark of the altricial growth strategy. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period in this species, which center around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the fledgling reaches the critical developmental milestone of flight feather maturation at precisely 12.5 days since birth [tx = 12.5 days since birth] at fledging. This remarkably short post-hatching period is characteristic of many temperate-zone passerines, reflecting the selective pressure to depart the nest and escape predation risk. The time since birth at fledging (12.5 days since birth) [tx = 12.5 days since birth] is notably brief compared to the total pre-reproductive phase, underscoring a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid early development over extended parental care at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Parental provisioning by both the male and female continues for some days after the fledgling leaves the nest, during which the young bird learns to capture prey independently while still relying on adults for a portion of its dietary intake.

Sexual maturation in the Dunnock proceeds relatively quickly after independence, with puberty occurring at 37.5 days since birth [tp = 37.5 days since birth] under thermoneutral conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This early attainment of reproductive capacity, measured in captive-reared birds, enables first-year individuals to participate in the complex mating system for which this species is well known. The age at puberty (37.5 days since birth) [tp = 37.5 days since birth] is considerably younger than that observed in many other small passerines of comparable adult mass, possibly reflecting an adaptation to the unpredictable food availability of the Dunnock's woodland-edge and hedgerow habitats at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The onset of gonadal swelling and the associated testosterone surge are triggered by increasing photoperiod in spring, but the underlying physiological capacity for reproduction is established by approximately 37.5 days since birth [tp = approximately 37.5 days since birth] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. However, under average field conditions, most young birds delay actual breeding until the following season, as they must first establish a territory and secure a mate.

First reproduction in the Dunnock is typically deferred until the spring following the year of hatching, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days] when maintained at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This interval reflects the need for juvenile birds to undergo a complete pre-basic molt, accumulate sufficient lipid stores to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation, and navigate the social complexities of the breeding system. This reproductive schedule yields a maximum reproductive rate that, over the course of a full year, equates to roughly five young per 365 days under optimal conditions, a figure consistent with the species' status as a multibrooded temperate passerine.

The maximum lifespan of the Dunnock has been documented at 11 years [am = 11 years] in wild populations, with the oldest recorded individuals persisting under the metabolic conditions associated with a core body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Basal metabolic rate, measured at rest in post-absorptive adults under thermoneutral conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reaches 58.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 58.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns well with allometric predictions for a passerine of this body size. Female asymptotic mass settles at 20.05 grams [Wwi = 20.05 grams], while their male counterparts, averaging 20.7 grams [Wwi = 20.7 grams], exhibit a modest size advantage of approximately 3 percent; this small degree of sexual size dimorphism, typical of many monogamous and polygynandrous passerines, is thought to relate more to intrasexual competition among males than to differential parental investment.
